extraction_notes.note: Lecture-note style blueprint of standard Schwartz distribution theory with no citations; following Hard rule 3, standard definitions and results are origin external 'standard (uncited)', while examples, the notes' own remarks and all proofs are paper. As a consequence no rigor field is set, even on PrP4 whose only proof is a 'Sketch.'.
Remark environments that define notions (sequential convergence structure, weak derivative); retyped to definition.
Example environments: Lambda f and the Dirac delta define objects used throughout, retyped to definition; 'delta is not a function' is followed by a proof, retyped to claim.
One-sentence 'we automatically have the inversion theorem ... because it holds for test functions'; kept as a named external theorem rather than a remark, the justification stays in its span.
Sentences in the Laplacian and heat-operator subsections lack terminal punctuation after displays; spans follow the apparent sentence groups.

The heat-kernel derivation sentence 'We have (d/dt) H_t^ = ... obviously solved by ...' and the convention 'In this chapter we may omit the Lambda' got no nodes (motivation/convention); chapter 1 'Analysis in Mathlib' is empty.
'Now define F(x,t) := ...' has no period after its display, so the following temperedness assertion is part of the same sentence and the same definition node.
Schwartz space is introduced informally in prose and then formally in Definition 3; treated as one node with the prose copy in also_stated_at.

nodes.name: Test functions and distributions
nodes.statement: $\cD(\Omega) = C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is the set of test functions together with a topology determined by its converging sequences : $\phi_n \to \phi$ in $\cD(\Omega)$ if \begin{itemize} \item there exists a compact subset $K \subset \Omega$ such that $\Supp(\phi_n) \subset K$. \item For all multiindices $\alpha$ we have $\partial_\alpha \phi_n \to \partial_\alpha \phi$ in uniformly. \end{itemize} Convention: if $x \in \R^d \setminus \Omega$, then $\phi(x) := 0$.\\ $\cD'(\Omega)$ is the topological dual space, i.e. the space of continuous linear functionals $D(\Omega) \to \C$ with the weak-*-convergence, i.e. pointwise convergence.
nodes.statement_short: $\cD(\Omega)$: compactly supported smooth functions with sequential convergence; $\cD'(\Omega)$: continuous linear functionals on it with weak-* convergence.

nodes.name: Notion of converging sequence
nodes.statement: A notion of converging sequence on a set $X$ is \begin{itemize} \item The constant function on $x$ converges to $x$ \item A sequence converges to $x$ iff any subsequence has a subsequence converging to $x$. \end{itemize} Note, that any subsequence of a converging sequence converges to the same limit. It induces a closure operator on $X$ (for $\overline{A \cup B} \subset \bar A \cup \bar B$ you use, that if a sequence in $A \cup B$ converges to $x$, then it has a subsequence (converging to $x$) lying in $A$ or in $B$).
nodes.statement_short: Axioms for a sequential convergence structure on a set; it induces a closure operator.

nodes.name: Distribution of a locally integrable function
nodes.statement: Every locally integrable function $f \in L^1_{loc}(\Omega)$ gives us a distribution $\Lambda f \in D'(\Omega)$ defined by \[ \Lambda f (\phi) = \int_{\Omega} f(x) \phi(x) \dm x \] which is well-defined because $\phi$ has compact support.
nodes.statement_short: A locally integrable $f$ defines the distribution $\Lambda f(\phi)=\int f\phi$.

nodes.name: Radon measures as distributions
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a Radon measure on $\Omega$ (or more generally a signed Borel measure which is finite on compact subsets of $\Omega$). Then it defines a distribution: \[ T_\mu(\phi) = \int_{\Omega} \phi \dm \mu \]

nodes.name: Radon measure defines a distribution
nodes.statement: Then it defines a distribution: \[ T_\mu(\phi) = \int_{\Omega} \phi \dm \mu \]

nodes.name: Proof that a Radon measure defines a distribution
nodes.statement: As Borel sets are $\mu$-measurable, every continuous function is $\mu$-measurable. Let $K := \Supp \phi \subset \Omega $. Because $\mu(K) < \infty$ and $\max \phi(K) < \infty$ it follows that $\phi$ is $\mu$-integrable. Linearity follows from linearity of the integral. If $\phi_j \to \phi_*$ unifomrly, then $\Supp \phi_j \subset K$ for all $j$ and $T_\mu \phi_j \to \Lambda_\mu \phi_*$.
nodes.statement_short: Check measurability, integrability on the compact support, linearity and continuity directly.

nodes.name: Measurability
nodes.statement: As Borel sets are $\mu$-measurable, every continuous function is $\mu$-measurable.
nodes.statement_short: Continuous functions are $\mu$-measurable.

nodes.name: Integrability
nodes.statement: Let $K := \Supp \phi \subset \Omega $. Because $\mu(K) < \infty$ and $\max \phi(K) < \infty$ it follows that $\phi$ is $\mu$-integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Finite measure of the compact support gives integrability.

nodes.name: Linearity
nodes.statement: Linearity follows from linearity of the integral.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity from linearity of the integral.

nodes.name: Continuity
nodes.statement: If $\phi_j \to \phi_*$ unifomrly, then $\Supp \phi_j \subset K$ for all $j$ and $T_\mu \phi_j \to \Lambda_\mu \phi_*$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform convergence with common support gives continuity.

nodes.name: Dirac delta distribution
nodes.statement: We have $\delta \in D'(\Omega)$ given by \[ \delta(\phi) := \phi(0) \]

nodes.name: Reflection and shift of test functions
nodes.statement: For $\phi \in D$ define $\phi^R \in D$ as $\phi^R(x) = \phi(-x)$ and for $x \in \R^d$ we have the shift $\tau_x(\phi) \in D$ given by $\tau_x(\phi)(y) = \phi(y - x)$ .
nodes.statement_short: Reflection $\phi^R(x)=\phi(-x)$ and translation $\tau_x\phi(y)=\phi(y-x)$.

nodes.name: Convolution of a function as a distribution evaluation
nodes.statement: {} For $f \in L^1_{loc}(\Omega), g \in D(\Omega)$ we have \[ (f * g)(x) = \Lambda f (\tau_x (\psi^R)) \]
nodes.statement_short: Ordinary convolution $f*g$ evaluated at $x$ equals $\Lambda f$ applied to a shifted reflection.
nodes.label: ex:conv

nodes.name: Convolution of a distribution with a test function
nodes.statement: Let $F \in \cD'(\Omega) , \psi \in D$. The following two distributions coincide: \begin{enumerate} \item The distribution determined by the smooth function $x \mapsto F(\tau_x (\psi^R))$. \item The distribution $\phi \mapsto F(\psi^R * \phi)$. \end{enumerate} We write this distribution as $F * \psi$.
conclusions: The following two distributions coincide: \begin{enumerate} \item The distribution determined by the smooth function $x \mapsto F(\tau_x (\psi^R))$. \item The distribution $\phi \mapsto F(\psi^R * \phi)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For a distribution $F$ and test function $\psi$, $x\mapsto F(\tau_x\psi^R)$ and $\phi\mapsto F(\psi^R*\phi)$ define the same distribution $F*\psi$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: $\zeta := \psi^R$ The function $x \mapsto F(\tau_x(\psi^R))$ is smooth : \begin{itemize} \item It is continuous: If $x_n \to x$, then $\tau_x (\zeta) - \tau_{x_n}(\zeta) \to 0 $ uniformly and the same holds for partial derivatives. Now $F$ is continuous hence $F(\tau_{\bullet}(\psi^R))$ is continuous and $F$ preserves the difference quotients, hence it will be also smooth. \item The two distributions coincide: \begin{align*} F(\psi^R * \phi) &= F \left(\int(\tau_x \psi^R(\bullet) \phi(x) \dm x) \right) \\ &\overset{!}{=} \int F(\tau_x \psi^R(\bullet) \phi(x)) \dm x \\ &= \int F(\tau_x \psi^R) \phi(x) \dm x \\ &= \Lambda(F(\tau_{\bullet} \psi^R))(\phi) \end{align*} Where we are allowed to pull out the integral by \ref{lemma:distribCommInt} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Show smoothness via continuity of $F$ and difference quotients, then commute $F$ with the integral (Lemma 1) to identify both distributions.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: $\zeta := \psi^R$ The function $x \mapsto F(\tau_x(\psi^R))$ is smooth :
nodes.statement_short: Set $\zeta=\psi^R$; claim smoothness.

nodes.name: Smoothness
nodes.statement: It is continuous: If $x_n \to x$, then $\tau_x (\zeta) - \tau_{x_n}(\zeta) \to 0 $ uniformly and the same holds for partial derivatives. Now $F$ is continuous hence $F(\tau_{\bullet}(\psi^R))$ is continuous and $F$ preserves the difference quotients, hence it will be also smooth.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity and smoothness from continuity of $F$.

nodes.name: Coincidence
nodes.statement: The two distributions coincide: \begin{align*} F(\psi^R * \phi) &= F \left(\int(\tau_x \psi^R(\bullet) \phi(x) \dm x) \right) \\ &\overset{!}{=} \int F(\tau_x \psi^R(\bullet) \phi(x)) \dm x \\ &= \int F(\tau_x \psi^R) \phi(x) \dm x \\ &= \Lambda(F(\tau_{\bullet} \psi^R))(\phi) \end{align*} Where we are allowed to pull out the integral by \ref{lemma:distribCommInt}
nodes.statement_short: Pull $F$ through the integral to identify the distributions.

nodes.name: Distributions commute with integration
nodes.statement: {} Let $\phi \in C_c^{\infty}(\Omega \times \Omega)$. Then for any $F \in D'(\Omega)$ we have \[ F \left(\int_\Omega \phi(x,\_) \dm x \right) = \int_\Omega F(\phi(x ,\_)) \dm x \]
nodes.statement_short: A distribution can be pulled inside a parameter integral of a test function.
nodes.label: lemma:distribCommInt

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Consider $S_\varepsilon \in D$ defined by \[S_\varepsilon^\phi(y) = \varepsilon^d \sum_{n \in \Z^d} \phi(n \varepsilon,y)\] which is a finite sum as $\phi$ has compact support. Then for all $\phi \in C_c^\infty(\Omega \times \Omega)$ one has a limit in $\cD$ \[ \int_\Omega \phi(x,\_) \dm x = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} S^\phi_\varepsilon \] Hence by continuity of $F$ \begin{align*} F(\int_\Omega \phi(x,\_) \dm x) &= F(\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} S^\phi_\varepsilon) \\ &= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} F(S^{\phi}_\varepsilon) \\ &= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon^d \sum_{n \in \Z^d} F(\phi(n \varepsilon,\_)) \\ &= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} S^{F \circ \phi}_\varepsilon \\ &= \int_\Omega F(\phi(x,\_)) \dm x \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Approximate the integral by Riemann sums $S_\varepsilon$ converging in $\cD$, then use continuity and linearity of $F$.

nodes.name: Riemann sums
nodes.statement: Consider $S_\varepsilon \in D$ defined by \[S_\varepsilon^\phi(y) = \varepsilon^d \sum_{n \in \Z^d} \phi(n \varepsilon,y)\] which is a finite sum as $\phi$ has compact support.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce Riemann sums $S_\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Convergence in D
nodes.statement: Then for all $\phi \in C_c^\infty(\Omega \times \Omega)$ one has a limit in $\cD$ \[ \int_\Omega \phi(x,\_) \dm x = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} S^\phi_\varepsilon \]
nodes.statement_short: Riemann sums converge to the integral in $\cD$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence by continuity of $F$ \begin{align*} F(\int_\Omega \phi(x,\_) \dm x) &= F(\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} S^\phi_\varepsilon) \\ &= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} F(S^{\phi}_\varepsilon) \\ &= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon^d \sum_{n \in \Z^d} F(\phi(n \varepsilon,\_)) \\ &= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} S^{F \circ \phi}_\varepsilon \\ &= \int_\Omega F(\phi(x,\_)) \dm x \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use continuity of $F$ to pass the limit.

nodes.name: Unambiguous convolution notation
nodes.statement: From the description \ref{ex:conv}: Writing $\Lambda f * g$ is unambiguous.

nodes.name: Convolution with the Dirac delta
nodes.statement: We have $\delta_0 * f = \Lambda f$ for all $f \in D$.

nodes.name: Continuity of convolution
nodes.statement: {} Convolution $F * \psi$ is continuous in both variables.
conclusions: Convolution $F * \psi$ is continuous in both variables.
nodes.label: lemma:cont

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Continuity in the distribution variable is clear by pointwise convergence. \\ For the continuity in the test function variable one uses that convolution with a fixed test function is a continuous function $\cD \to \cD$ and distributions are continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise convergence in the distribution; continuity of convolution $\cD\to\cD$ in the test function.

nodes.name: Delta is in the closure of test functions
nodes.statement: {} There exists a sequence $\psi_n \in C_c^{\infty}(\Omega)$ such that $\Lambda \psi_n \to \delta_0$ in $D'(\Omega)$.
conclusions: There exists a sequence $\psi_n \in C_c^{\infty}(\Omega)$ such that $\Lambda \psi_n \to \delta_0$ in $D'(\Omega)$.
nodes.statement_short: An approximate identity $\psi_n$ gives $\Lambda\psi_n\to\delta_0$.
nodes.label: proposition:deltaInClosure

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Fix some $\psi \in D$ with $\int \psi(x) \dm x = 1$. Define $\psi_n (x) := n^d \psi(nx)$. Then \[ (\Lambda \psi_n - \delta_0) (\phi ) = \int n^d \psi (n x) \phi(x) \dm x - \phi(0) = \int \psi (x) \cdot (\phi(x / n) - \phi(0)) \dm x \to 0 \] where we used that $\phi(x/n) - \phi(0) \to 0$ uniformly. \\
nodes.statement_short: Construct the approximate identity $\psi_n(x)=n^d\psi(nx)$ and change variables.

nodes.name: Approximate identity
nodes.statement: Fix some $\psi \in D$ with $\int \psi(x) \dm x = 1$. Define $\psi_n (x) := n^d \psi(nx)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define rescaled bumps $\psi_n$.

nodes.name: Convergence
nodes.statement: Then \[ (\Lambda \psi_n - \delta_0) (\phi ) = \int n^d \psi (n x) \phi(x) \dm x - \phi(0) = \int \psi (x) \cdot (\phi(x / n) - \phi(0)) \dm x \to 0 \] where we used that $\phi(x/n) - \phi(0) \to 0$ uniformly.
nodes.statement_short: Change variables and use uniform convergence.

nodes.name: Locally integrable functions are determined by their distributions
nodes.statement: Let $f,g \in L^1_{loc}(\Omega)$ such that $\Lambda_f = \Lambda_g$. Then $f = g$ almost everywhere.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: We have $0 = \Lambda(f-g)(\tau_{\bullet} \psi_n^R) = \psi_n * (f - g) \to \delta_0 * (f-g) = f-g$ in $L^1_{loc}$, hence $f = g$ almost everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: Convolve $f-g$ with the approximate identity and pass to the limit in $L^1_{loc}$.

nodes.name: Dirac delta is not a function
nodes.statement: $\delta$ is not a function! I.e. its not of the form $\Lambda f$ for some $f \in L^1_{loc}$
conclusions: $\delta$ is not a function! I.e. its not of the form $\Lambda f$ for some $f \in L^1_{loc}$

nodes.name: Proof that delta is not a function
nodes.statement: We have $\Delta|_{\Omega \setminus \{0\}}= \Lambda 0$ so if it would be a function, then it would be zero almost everywhere, hence 0. But this is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Away from 0 delta vanishes, so a representing function would be zero a.e.; contradiction.

nodes.name: Smooth functions are dense in distributions
nodes.statement: Then $C^\infty(\R^d)$ is dense in $\cD'(\R^d)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2
nodes.statement: We know by \ref{proposition:deltaInClosure} that there exists $\Lambda \psi_n \to \delta_0$ in $\cD'$. Let $F$ be a distribution on $\R^d$. Now setting $F_n := F * \psi_n^R$ , yields pointwise \[ F_n(\phi) = F (\psi_n * \phi) \to F(\delta_0 * \phi) = F (\phi) \] by \ref{lemma:cont} hence $F_n \to F$ in $\cD'$.
nodes.statement_short: Regularize $F$ by convolution with the approximate identity and use continuity of convolution.

nodes.name: Recall
nodes.statement: We know by \ref{proposition:deltaInClosure} that there exists $\Lambda \psi_n \to \delta_0$ in $\cD'$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the approximate identity.

nodes.name: Mollify
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a distribution on $\R^d$. Now setting $F_n := F * \psi_n^R$ , yields pointwise \[ F_n(\phi) = F (\psi_n * \phi) \to F(\delta_0 * \phi) = F (\phi) \] by \ref{lemma:cont} hence $F_n \to F$ in $\cD'$.
nodes.statement_short: Mollify $F$ and pass to the limit.

nodes.name: Integration by parts for test functions
nodes.statement: For $\phi , \psi \in D$ we have \[ \int_\Omega \partial^\alpha \phi \psi \dm x = (-1)^{|\alpha|} \int_\Omega \phi \partial^\alpha \psi \dm x \]

nodes.name: Distributional derivative
nodes.statement: For a multiindex $\alpha$ and a distribution $F$ define the distribution \[\partial^\alpha F (\phi) = (-1)^{|\alpha|}(F \partial^\alpha \phi)\]

nodes.name: Weak derivative
nodes.statement: let $f \in L^1_{loc}(\Omega)$. If there exists some $f' \in L^1_{loc}(\Omega)$, such that $\Lambda f' = \partial^\alpha \Lambda f$ as distributions, then we call $f'$ the {\bf weak derivative} of $f$ with respect to $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Derivatives commute with convolution
nodes.statement: For $F \in D', \phi \in D $ , We have \[\partial^\alpha (F * \phi) = (\partial^\alpha F) * \phi = F * \partial^\alpha \phi\]

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: First note, that holds in the case where $F$ is a test function, so that we have ordinary convolution. Then check pointwise. After erasing the sign $(-1)^{|\alpha|}$ \[ F(\phi^R * \partial^\alpha \psi) = F(\partial^\alpha (\phi^R * \psi)) = F((\partial^\alpha \phi) * \psi) \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to ordinary convolution of test functions and check pointwise.

nodes.name: Test function case
nodes.statement: First note, that holds in the case where $F$ is a test function, so that we have ordinary convolution.
nodes.statement_short: Holds for test functions.

nodes.name: Pointwise check
nodes.statement: Then check pointwise. After erasing the sign $(-1)^{|\alpha|}$ \[ F(\phi^R * \partial^\alpha \psi) = F(\partial^\alpha (\phi^R * \psi)) = F((\partial^\alpha \phi) * \psi) \]
nodes.statement_short: Check pointwise using the sign convention.

nodes.name: Support of a distribution
nodes.statement: The Support of a distribution $F$ is the complement of the largest open subset $U$, such that $F(\phi) = 0 \forall \phi \in D, \Supp(\phi) \subset U$.
nodes.genus: the complement of the largest open subset $U$

nodes.name: Support is well defined
nodes.statement: This definition is unambiguous: If $F$ vanishes on each $U_i$ for some index set $I$ and $\phi \in D$ such that the compact set $\Supp \phi \subset U = \bigcup U_i$, we may assume that $I$ is finite and choose a partition of unity $\Supp \eta_i \subset U_i$ and $\sum \eta_i = 1$. Then $F(\phi) = \sum F(\phi \eta_i) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Partition of unity shows a distribution vanishing on each $U_i$ vanishes on their union.

nodes.name: Schwartz space
nodes.statement: Consider the increasing sequence of norms on $C^\infty(\Omega)$ defined by \[ \|\phi\|_N = \sup \{ | x^\beta (\partial_x^\alpha \phi(x)) | \mid x \in \R^d , |\alpha|,\|\beta\|\le N\} \] \[ \cS = \{\phi \in C^\infty(\R^d) \mid \|\phi\|_N < \infty \forall N\} \] with the obvious notion of convergence.
also_stated_at: We no enlarge our test space to the schwartz space $\cS = \cS(\R^d)$ consisting of smooth functions that are rapidly decreasing at $\infty$ with all derivatives.
nodes.statement_short: Smooth functions with all seminorms $\sup|x^\beta\partial^\alpha\phi|$ finite.

nodes.name: Tempered distributions are distributions
nodes.statement: We have a continuous inclusions $\cD \subset \cS$, hence $\cS' \subset \cD'(\R^d)$. \\ Moreover, this inclusion is dense. Hence being tempered is a property of distributions.
conclusions: We have a continuous inclusions $\cD \subset \cS$, hence $\cS' \subset \cD'(\R^d)$.

nodes.name: Polynomially growing functions are tempered
nodes.statement: {} Let $f \in L^1_{loc}(\R^d)$ such that there exists $N \ge 0$ with \[ \int_{|x| < R} |f(x)| \dm x = O(R^N) , \text{ as } R \to \infty \] The distribution $\Lambda_f$ is tempered.
assumptions: Let $f \in L^1_{loc}(\R^d)$ such that there exists $N \ge 0$ with \[ \int_{|x| < R} |f(x)| \dm x = O(R^N) , \text{ as } R \to \infty \]
nodes.label: lemma:slowlyInc

nodes.name: Lp functions are tempered
nodes.statement: This condition holds for functions in $L^p(\R^d)$ for $p \in [1,\infty]$

nodes.name: Compactly supported distributions are tempered
nodes.statement: If $F \in \cD'$ has compact support then it is tempered: Choose $\eta \in \cD$ such that $\eta|_U = 1$ on some neighborhood $U \supset \Supp(F)$. Then $F(\eta \phi) = F(\phi)$ for all $\phi \in \cD$ and $\phi \mapsto F (\eta \phi)$ defines a continuous functional on $\cS$. It does not depend on the choice of $\eta$, because given another such $\eta'$ and any $\phi \in \cS$ we have $\Supp((\eta - \eta') \cdot \phi) \cap \Supp(F) = \varnothing$.
nodes.statement_short: A compactly supported distribution extends to $\cS$ via a cutoff $\eta$, independent of the cutoff.

nodes.name: Tempered distribution F
nodes.statement: Let $F$ denote a tempered distribution.

nodes.name: Stability of tempered distributions
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item All $\partial^\alpha F$ are tempered. \item Let $\psi \in C^\infty$ be slowly increasing, i.e. for each $\alpha$ exists $N_\alpha$ such that $\partial_x^\alpha \psi(x) = O(|x|^{N_\alpha})$. Then $\psi F$, defined by $(\psi F)(\phi)(F(\psi \phi)$ is tempered. \end{itemize}
assumptions: Let $\psi \in C^\infty$ be slowly increasing, i.e. for each $\alpha$ exists $N_\alpha$ such that $\partial_x^\alpha \psi(x) = O(|x|^{N_\alpha})$.
conclusions: Then $\psi F$, defined by $(\psi F)(\phi)(F(\psi \phi)$ is tempered.
nodes.statement_short: Derivatives and products with slowly increasing smooth functions of tempered distributions are tempered.

assumptions: Let $\psi \in C^\infty$ be slowly increasing, i.e. for each $\alpha$ exists $N_\alpha$ such that $\partial_x^\alpha \psi(x) = O(|x|^{N_\alpha})$.
conclusions: Then $\psi F$, defined by $(\psi F)(\phi)(F(\psi \phi)$ is tempered.

nodes.name: Convolution with Schwartz functions
nodes.statement: If $\psi \in \cS$, then $F(\tau_\bullet (\psi^R))$ is slowly increasing. The other formulation is still valid because $\cS$ is stable under $*$.

nodes.name: Fourier transform on Schwartz space
nodes.statement: The fourier transformation is a continuous bijection \begin{align*} \cS &\to \cS \\ \phi &\mapsto \hat \phi = (\xi \mapsto \int_{\R^d} \phi(x) e^{-2\pi i x \xi} \dm x) \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Fourier transform $\hat\phi(\xi)=\int\phi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$, a continuous bijection of $\cS$.

nodes.name: Fourier transform is self-adjoint
nodes.statement: We have \[\Lambda_{\hat \psi}(\phi) = \int_{\R^d} \hat \psi (x) \phi(x) \dm x = \int_{\R^d} \psi(x) \hat \phi(x) \dm x = \Lambda_{\psi}(\hat \phi)\]
nodes.statement_short: $\int\hat\psi\phi=\int\psi\hat\phi$ (multiplication formula).

nodes.name: Fourier transform of tempered distributions
nodes.statement: Define \[ \hat F (\phi) = F (\hat \phi) \] and similarly for the inverse transform $f \mapsto \check{f}$.

nodes.name: Fourier inversion theorem for distributions
nodes.statement: We automatically have the inversion theorem for distributions, because it holds for test functions.
conclusions: We automatically have the inversion theorem for distributions

nodes.name: Fourier transform of the Dirac delta
nodes.statement: If $1 \in S$ denotes the constant function at $1$, then \[ \widehat {\delta} = \Lambda_1 \] because \[ \hat \delta (\phi) =\hat \phi(0) = \int 1 \phi(x) \dm x = \Lambda_1(\phi) \]

nodes.name: Linear partial differential operator L
nodes.statement: Fix a partial differential operator $L$ \[ L = \sum_{|\alpha|\le m } a_\alpha \partial^\alpha \text { on } \R^d \] with $a_\alpha \in \C$.

nodes.name: Fundamental solution
nodes.statement: A fundamental solution of $L$ is a distribution $F$ such that $L(F) = \delta$

nodes.name: Convolution with a fundamental solution inverts L
nodes.statement: The operator \[ f \mapsto T(f) := F * f \] defines an inverse to $L$
conclusions: The operator \[ f \mapsto T(f) := F * f \] defines an inverse to $L$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement: because \[ \partial^\alpha (F * f) = (\partial^\alpha F) * f = F * (\partial^\alpha f) \] Summing over $\alpha$ gives \[ L(F * f) = \delta * f = F * L f \] Now recall $\delta * f = f$.
nodes.statement_short: Derivatives commute with convolution; sum over $\alpha$ and use $\delta*f=f$.

nodes.name: Commute
nodes.statement: because \[ \partial^\alpha (F * f) = (\partial^\alpha F) * f = F * (\partial^\alpha f) \]
nodes.statement_short: Derivatives commute with convolution.

nodes.name: Sum
nodes.statement: Summing over $\alpha$ gives \[ L(F * f) = \delta * f = F * L f \]
nodes.statement_short: Sum over multiindices.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Now recall $\delta * f = f$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $\delta*f=f$.

nodes.name: Characteristic polynomial
nodes.statement: The characteristic polynomial of $L$ is \[P(\xi) = \sum_{|\alpha|\le m} a_\alpha (2 \pi i \xi)^\alpha\]

nodes.name: Fourier transform diagonalizes L
nodes.statement: It is defined it such a way, that $\widehat{L f} = P \cdot \hat f$.

nodes.name: Heuristic fundamental solution via Fourier inversion
nodes.statement: So our hope is \[F := \widecheck{1 / (P (\xi))} = \int \frac{1}{P(\xi)} e^{2 \pi i x \xi} \dm \xi\] The problem is, that the zeros of $P$ result in difficulties to define $F$, even as a distribution.
nodes.statement_short: Candidate $F$ is the inverse Fourier transform of $1/P$, problematic at zeros of $P$.

nodes.name: Laplacian
nodes.statement: If $L = \Delta = \sum_{i=1}^d \frac{\partial^2}{\partial^2 x_i}$ So $1 / P (\xi) = 1 / (-4 \pi^2 |\xi|^2) $ which lies in $L^1_{loc}$ for $d \ge 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Laplacian $\Delta=\sum\partial_i^2$, whose symbol $1/(-4\pi^2|\xi|^2)$ is locally integrable for $d\ge3$.

nodes.name: Fourier transform of homogeneous functions |x|^lambda
nodes.statement: For $\lambda > -d$, Let $H_\lambda$ be the tempered distribution associated to $|x|^\lambda \in L^1_{loc}$. \\ If $-d < \lambda < 0$ then \[ \widehat {H_\lambda} = c_\lambda H_{-d-\lambda} \] with \[ c_\lambda = \frac{\Gamma((d + \lambda)/2)}{\Gamma(\lambda / 2)} \pi^{-d/2-\lambda} \]
assumptions: For $\lambda > -d$, Let $H_\lambda$ be the tempered distribution associated to $|x|^\lambda \in L^1_{loc}$.
nodes.statement_short: The Fourier transform of $|x|^\lambda$ is $c_\lambda|x|^{-d-\lambda}$ with an explicit Gamma-function constant.

nodes.name: Fundamental solution of the Laplacian for d >= 3
nodes.statement: Set $\lambda:=-d+2$. Hence we can find an appropriate constant $C_d$ such that $F(x) = C_d |x|^{-d +2}$ is a fundamental solution, because $\hat {F}(\xi) = 1 / (-4\pi^2|\xi|^2)$. So writing out $\widehat{\Delta F} = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: For $d\ge3$, $C_d|x|^{2-d}$ is a fundamental solution of $\Delta$ by Theorem 1 with $\lambda=2-d$.

nodes.name: Logarithmic fundamental solution in the plane
nodes.statement: If $d = 2$, the function $F := 1/(2\pi) \log |x| \in L^1_{loc}$ is a fundamental solution of $\Delta$
conclusions: the function $F := 1/(2\pi) \log |x| \in L^1_{loc}$ is a fundamental solution of $\Delta$

nodes.name: Sketch of proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement: Sketch. One can actually compute $\hat F = -1 / (4\pi^2) \left [\frac{1}{|x|^2} \right] - c' \delta$ for some constant $c'$, where $\left [\frac{1}{|x|^2} \right]$ is a distribution, that replaces the (non locally integrable) function $1 / |x|^2$ in an appropriate way: \[ \left [\frac{1}{|x|^2} \right] = \int_{|x| \le 1} \frac{\phi(x) - \phi(0)}{|x|^2} \dm x + \int_{|x| > 1} \frac{\phi(x)}{|x|^2} \dm x \] Notice, that on the complement of zero, this distribution coincides with $1 / |x|^2$. \begin{notation} If $\phi \in C^\infty(\Omega)$ slowly increasing (i.e. all derivatives are bounded by polynomials), define $\phi F \in \cS'$ as $\phi F(\psi) = F(\phi \psi)$. \end{notation} \begin{align*} \widehat{ \Delta F} &= -4 \pi^2 |x|^2 \hat F\\ &= |x|^2 \left [\frac{1}{|x|^2} \right] - 4\pi^2 c' \underbrace{|x|^2 \delta}_{=0} \\ &= 1 \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: compute $\hat F$ via the regularized distribution $[1/|x|^2]$ and multiply by $-4\pi^2|x|^2$.

nodes.name: Fourier transform of F
nodes.statement: Sketch. One can actually compute $\hat F = -1 / (4\pi^2) \left [\frac{1}{|x|^2} \right] - c' \delta$ for some constant $c'$, where $\left [\frac{1}{|x|^2} \right]$ is a distribution, that replaces the (non locally integrable) function $1 / |x|^2$ in an appropriate way: \[ \left [\frac{1}{|x|^2} \right] = \int_{|x| \le 1} \frac{\phi(x) - \phi(0)}{|x|^2} \dm x + \int_{|x| > 1} \frac{\phi(x)}{|x|^2} \dm x \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\hat F$ with the regularized $[1/|x|^2]$.

nodes.name: Away from zero
nodes.statement: Notice, that on the complement of zero, this distribution coincides with $1 / |x|^2$.
nodes.statement_short: The regularization agrees with $1/|x|^2$ away from 0.

nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement: \begin{notation} If $\phi \in C^\infty(\Omega)$ slowly increasing (i.e. all derivatives are bounded by polynomials), define $\phi F \in \cS'$ as $\phi F(\psi) = F(\phi \psi)$. \end{notation}
nodes.statement_short: Notation for multiplication by slowly increasing functions.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \widehat{ \Delta F} &= -4 \pi^2 |x|^2 \hat F\\ &= |x|^2 \left [\frac{1}{|x|^2} \right] - 4\pi^2 c' \underbrace{|x|^2 \delta}_{=0} \\ &= 1 \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $-4\pi^2|x|^2$ to get $\widehat{\Delta F}=1$.

nodes.name: Product of a slowly increasing function and a tempered distribution
nodes.statement: If $\phi \in C^\infty(\Omega)$ slowly increasing (i.e. all derivatives are bounded by polynomials), define $\phi F \in \cS'$ as $\phi F(\psi) = F(\phi \psi)$.

nodes.name: Initial value problem for the heat equation
nodes.statement: $L = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} - \Delta_x$ taken over $(x,t) \in \R^{d+1} = \R^d \times \R$ i.e. we want to solve the homogeneous initial value problem \[ \begin{cases} L (u) = 0 & , t > 0 \\ u(x,0) = f(x) & , t = 0 \end{cases} \] for some initial value $f \in \cS$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve $u_t=\Delta u$ for $t>0$ with $u(\cdot,0)=f\in\cS$.

nodes.name: Heat kernel
nodes.statement: We may call this the heat kernel \[ \hat{\cH_t}(\xi) = e^{-4\pi^2 |\xi|^2 t} \]

nodes.name: Heat kernel solves the initial value problem
nodes.statement: Note that for $t = 0$, we have $\hat{\cH_0} = 1$, hence $\cH_0 = \delta$, so $u(x,t) = (\cH * f)(x)$ solves the equation $L(u) = 0$ and $u(x,t) \to f(x)$ in $\cS$ as $t \to 0$.
conclusions: $u(x,t) = (\cH * f)(x)$ solves the equation $L(u) = 0$ and $u(x,t) \to f(x)$ in $\cS$ as $t \to 0$

nodes.name: Heat kernel is an approximate identity
nodes.statement: {} $\cH_t \to \delta$ in $\cS'$ as $t \to 0$ and $\int_{\R^d} \cH_t(x) \dm x = 1$ for all $t$
nodes.label: remark:approxId

nodes.name: Fundamental solution of the heat operator
nodes.statement: Now define \[ F(x,t) := \begin{cases} \cH_t(x) & , \ if \ t > 0 , \\ 0 & , t \le 0 \end{cases} \] $F$ is locally integrable on $\R^{d+1}$ and it actually holds \[ \int_{|t|\le R} \int_{\R^d} F(x,t) \dm x \dm t \le R \] so $F$ defines a tempered distribution by \ref{lemma:slowlyInc}.
nodes.statement_short: Define $F(x,t)=\cH_t(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0$ otherwise; it is locally integrable with polynomial growth, hence tempered.

nodes.name: Fundamental solution of the heat operator
nodes.statement: $F$ is a fundamental solution of $L = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} - \Delta_x$.
conclusions: $F$ is a fundamental solution of $L = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} - \Delta_x$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Denote $L' = - \frac{\partial}{\partial t} - \Delta_x$, then we have to see the last equation \[LF (\phi) = F(L'(\phi)) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \int_{t \ge \varepsilon} \int_{\R^d} F(x,t) ( -\frac{\partial}{\partial t} - \Delta_x) \phi(x,t) \dm x \dm t \overset{!}{=} \delta(\phi) \] Integration by parts \begin{align*} & \int_{t \ge \varepsilon} \int_{\R^d} F(x,t) ( -\frac{\partial}{\partial t} - \Delta_x) \phi(x,t) \dm x \dm t \\ &= - \int_{\R^d} \left(\int_{t \ge \varepsilon} \cH_t \frac{\partial}{\partial t} + (\Delta_x \cH_t) \phi \dm t \right) \dm x \\ &= - \int_{\R^d} \left(\int_{t \ge \varepsilon} \cH_t \frac{\partial}{\partial t} + ( \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \cH_t) \phi \dm t \right ) \dm x \\ &= \int_{\R^d} \cH_\varepsilon(x) \phi(x,\varepsilon) \dm x && \mid |\phi(x,\varepsilon) - \phi(x,0)| \le O(\varepsilon) \text{ uniformly in } x \\ &= \int_{\R^d} \cH_\varepsilon(x) (\phi(x,0) + O(\varepsilon)) \dm x && \ref{remark:approxId}\\ &\to \phi(0,0) \end{align*} where in the last line we let $\varepsilon \to 0$
nodes.statement_short: Cut off $t\ge\varepsilon$, integrate by parts using the heat equation for $\cH_t$, and let $\varepsilon\to0$ using the approximate identity.
